title: Cornell Chi Phi case: how a 2024 sexual assault report was handled
content_warning: This dive covers an alleged sexual assault, including references to drug and alcohol use and to statements the former student gave police. As of early October 2026, no one had been criminally charged.

question.prompt: Taken together, how would you rate the way Cornell, its police department and the Tompkins County DA's office handled the former student's 2024 sexual assault report?

starting_facts.text: On Sept. 16, 2026, a former Cornell student filed a civil lawsuit in New York State Supreme Court, New York County, alleging she was sexually assaulted by multiple people at the Chi Phi fraternity house on Oct. 19-20, 2024. The defendants include Cornell, Chi Phi fraternity entities and seven fraternity members.

starting_facts.text: In November 2024, Cornell police asked the Tompkins County DA's office to review a six-page statement the former student signed; AP and The New York Times report a police investigator wrote it from two days of interviews. The DA's office did not interview her and told police charges were not appropriate. The DA says the statement's facts, taken as true, showed no lack of consent under state law.

A former prosecutor told CNN the university likely did not break any laws if it did not share all relevant documents with the DA, but said not sharing them would violate 'all principles of what's logical and decent.' NPR asked Cornell whether its police gave the DA all the information from their investigation; Cornell did not respond. CNN, which obtained the six-page statement, reports that it does say part of the night 'felt like coercion' and that she was 'pretty incapacitated'; what ABC and the Times say it leaves out are the 'raped' lines.

depth.title: Where the transcript is

Cornell's FAQ says that before a Title IX investigation is finalized, the complainant and respondents, with their advisers, 'have an opportunity to review the full investigative record.' AP reported on Sept. 30, 2026 that the transcript had not been publicly released. That day, the DA told WSKG the transcript is part of Cornell's confidential Title IX investigation, that he was seeking it, and that he did not know when he would get it 'or if Cornell will resist turning it over.' depth.title: N.Y. Penal Law 130.00 (definitions)
depth.summary: Subsection 6 defines 'mentally incapacitated' as being temporarily unable to appraise or control one's conduct because of a narcotic or intoxicating substance given without consent, or because of any other act done without consent. Subsection 7 defines 'physically helpless' as being unconscious or for any other reason physically unable to communicate unwillingness. Subsection 8 defines 'forcible compulsion' as compelling by physical force or by certain threats.

depth.title: N.Y. Penal Law 130.05 (lack of consent)
depth.summary: Every sex offense in the article requires that the act was committed without the victim's consent. Lack of consent results from forcible compulsion or incapacity to consent; where the charge is sexual abuse or forcible touching, also from any circumstance in which the victim does not expressly or impliedly acquiesce; and, for certain third-degree rape charges, from the victim's clear expression of non-consent that a reasonable person in the actor's situation would have understood.

depth.title: The routes the DA's analysis lists
depth.body: The DA's Sept. 28 analysis lists four routes to lack of consent 'as it relates to this case': forcible compulsion, mental incapacitation, physical helplessness and, for certain charges, a clear expression of non-consent. Penal Law 130.05 also provides that, where the charge is sexual abuse or forcible touching, lack of consent can result from any circumstances in which the victim 'does not expressly or impliedly acquiesce' in the conduct. No source cited here applies that provision to this case.

evidence.quote: In this case, multiple prosecutors and criminal investigators reviewed Jane Doe's statement and correctly determined the alleged facts as set forth in the statement do not constitute a crime.

The facts provided by Jane Doe's statement do not allege that any person used physical force to compel Jane Doe to engage in sexual conduct.
The facts provided by Jane Doe's statement do not allege that she was either rendered incapable of controlling her own conduct or that any drug was administered to her without her consent.

sides.label: They acted reasonably on what they had
sides.steelman: On this view, Cornell and the DA's office acted on the record in front of them and within the law. Cornell suspended the chapter and alerted the campus the day she came forward, issued interim suspensions, and ran a Title IX case with more than 50 interviews and 12 days of hearings that ended in expulsions and suspensions, while federal privacy law limits what it can say about individual students. Campus police took a two-day interview and sent prosecutors a statement she reviewed, annotated and signed as true and correct; assuming every word was true, the DA's office applied New York's consent law as written, under which intoxication counts as mental incapacity only when the intoxicating substance is given without consent, and the DA says that, according to the statement, each time she asked to stop, 'the sexual conduct stopped.' The DA offered through campus police to meet her, heard nothing from her or her attorneys for nearly two years, reopened the case himself once the lawsuit described her consent differently, and backed the attorney general's appointment. On this view, the main problem is the law itself, which the governor, while faulting the institutions, also called 'a gap in State law.'

sides.label: The institutions fell short
sides.steelman: On this view, key steps were missed between her report and the decision not to charge. Campus police first recorded that she reported being raped by 8-10 men, and in a two-day interview she said she could say 'with 100% confidence' she was raped, that she was 'physically hit very, very hard' and 'completely and totally incapacitated,' and that 'it was coercion,' yet the six-page statement a police investigator condensed from roughly 120 pages of transcript and sent to prosecutors left out the 'raped' remarks. The DA's office decided within days without interviewing her or reading the transcript, did not take up further material when a Cornell investigator raised it, and police did not tell her of the decision for nearly two months, while Ithaca police were never told. Cornell then told the public its police had shared 'all investigatory information' and later dropped that line, some accused students received sanctions such as reflection papers, and the governor removed the DA, citing a statement that 'reportedly omitted key portions' of her account; the DA himself then said 'we were not provided the full picture by the University,' and Cornell's president said the university 'must do better.'

bias_reports.summary: Red-team read of /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Project1/4f5abf7d-ef16-5fee-841f-519f305d1748/scratchpad/cornell/work/draft-r2.json from the "They acted reasonably on what they had" side, ignoring the review field. The draft is careful at the sentence level. Claims are attributed. I found no judging adjectives outside direct quotes. Steps alternate between the sides, and impact is balanced: each side has three high-impact steps. The DA's key lines are present, including "credibility ... was never in question," "we do not conduct parallel independent investigations," and "evidence and not emotion." Several facts that help Cornell are also included: the AP "False" rating on "Cornell didn't follow up," the "Misleading" rating on the essay claim, the court ruling upholding Cornell's procedures, and the privacy law. The tilt is structural and comes from what was left out: 1. **Rebuttal ordering.** Steps 4, 6 and 8 favor my side, and each body ends with the other side's rebuttal. Step 4 ends with AP's "sparse redacted pieces." Steps 1 and 5 favor the other side and end with more criticism, with no rebuttal. 2. **Framing.** The dive opens with the 2026 transcript revelation instead of Cornell's same-day suspension. Its last steps are the governor's "was failed by people and institutions" and then the Ithaca permit pause. 3. **Confidence labels.** "Disputed" appears on three of my side's five steps and on none of the other side's. One of the three, consent-law-gap, rests mainly on statute text. 4. **Missing exculpatory facts.** These come from sources I opened in this run: - The Cornell FAQ says the chapter "was closed in 2024." - The DA's statement says CUPD asked his office to review whether the statement described a crime, which is "common practice." It also says forcible compulsion means force used "to compel" sexual conduct, and that "failure to remember certain events days later is not sufficient evidence of unconsciousness." - The AP fact check says the DA thought the statement was "detailed enough" and "appeared at the time to be a comprehensive account." - The NYT says the Title IX files, including the transcript, were "distributed in early 2025." The FAQ says the parties and their advisers "have an opportunity to review the full investigative record." - EO 64 cites concerns "raised, both by Jane Doe and the public," including "public perception," and identifies no actual conflict. 5. **Drafter's own legal theory.** The draft adds an argument that no source makes: that the DA's analysis skipped the sexual-abuse "acquiesce" route. It appears in a step's depth section and again in the open questions. 6. **Open questions.** Seven of the eight probe possible institutional failures. One flag is high severity (rebuttal ordering on step 4). The rest are medium or low.

After the DA's reading, the body closes with: "CNN and NBC News, which obtained the statement, report it also describes her being hit (...), being 'pretty incapacitated,' swatting one man's hand away several times, hiding because men stood between her and the exit, and that part of the night 'felt like coercion.' AP notes the DA's release included only 'sparse redacted pieces' of the statement, which has not been made public." Steps 6 and 8 follow the same pattern: acted-reasonably steps end with a rebuttal. Fell-short steps 1 and 5 end with more criticism instead: Cornell's later-withdrawn "shared all investigatory information" in step 1, and the mayor's "failed to contact or coordinate any response" in step 5. A reader on my side would see the dive repeatedly giving the other side the last word on our strongest points. Fix: put the counter-lines in the depth section, or end on the DA's "each time she asked to stop, the sexual conduct stopped," and apply the same structure to both sides.
flags.resolution: Step 4 body reordered: the lines CNN and NBC report from the statement now come before the DA's quoted lines and his 'the sexual conduct stopped' and memory-gap points, and the body ends on the neutral fact that the DA has not released the statement, citing a privacy review. Same rule applied elsewhere: step 6's ABC line moved mid-body; step 9 and step 12 no longer end on one side's rebuttal.

flags.note: The body lists the DA's first route as plain "physical force," then sets "being hit" against it, which implies the DA overlooked force. His actual test (DA statement, p. 7) is whether "any person used physical force to compel Jane Doe to engage in sexual conduct." Penal Law 130.00(8), which the draft cites, likewise says "compelling by physical force." The step also leaves out the DA's direct answer to the memory-gap point: "(The failure to remember certain events days later is not sufficient evidence of unconsciousness at the time.)" The draft cites her memory gaps in step 1 depth ("had gaps in her memory") and step 4 depth ("I don't remember much of this threesome") without that answer.
flags.resolution: Step 4 body now lists the force route as 'force used to compel sex' and adds the DA's point that memory gaps days later are 'not sufficient evidence of unconsciousness.'

flags.note: "AP notes the DA's release included only 'sparse redacted pieces' of the statement" adopts a dismissive description as the step's last sentence. The DA's Sept. 28 release gives about three pages to the statement's facts, quoting it directly, and explains why he did not release the full document: "a released copy of the statement would have to go through a privacy review and be heavily redacted." That explanation is only in the depth section. Suggested neutral wording: "The DA quoted from the statement at length but did not release it, citing privacy review and redaction."
flags.resolution: Step 4 body now ends: 'The DA has not released the statement, citing a privacy review.' AP's 'sparse redacted pieces' kept, attributed, in the statement-excerpts layer.

flags.note: The draft adds its own legal argument against the DA, which no source makes. Depth 'routes-in-da-analysis' says: "The DA's analysis does not discuss that route; the sources cited here do not say whether his office considered it" (the sexual-abuse 'does not expressly or impliedly acquiesce' route). Open question 3 repeats it: "including the sexual-abuse route the DA's analysis does not discuss." The only sources cited are the statute and the DA's statement, which lists its routes "as it relates to this case." Either attribute this argument to an identified expert or remove it.
flags.resolution: The routes layer now says only that the statute lists the acquiescence route for sexual abuse or forcible touching and that 'No source cited here applies that provision to this case.' Open question 3 no longer says the DA's analysis skips it.

flags.note: Opening and closing both go to the 'fell short' side. Step 1 is the most damaging 2026 revelation: "she told campus police she was raped; those lines were not in the six-page statement." The chronological starting point would be the Nov. 8, 2024 same-day chapter suspension and crime alert. The last argumentative step is the governor's removal of the DA, with Hochul's "was failed by people and institutions with an obligation to protect her." The final step's body then ends with "Ithaca's council voted 9-1 to pause new city permits for Cornell-affiliated events." Consider chronological order, or ending on a neutral status line.
flags.resolution: Partly changed: step 12 now ends on the pending reviews and CNN's four questions instead of the permit vote or the motion to void. The opening was kept: the starting facts already give the Nov. 8 chapter suspension and crime alert as the baseline, and step 1 is the central disputed handoff. Left to the owner (open issue).

flags.note: The draft treats the transcript's absence from the DA's file purely as a failure by Cornell to share it. It leaves out that the transcript was part of a record available to the parties. The NYT (cited as nyt-takeaways) says the files, including "an extensive transcript of the original police interviews," were "compiled for Cornell's Title IX administrative hearing process and distributed in early 2025." The Cornell FAQ (cornell-faq) says "the complainant and respondent(s), in conjunction with their advisors, have an opportunity to review the full investigative record." The DA says that in nearly two years neither she nor her attorneys contacted his office, "not to suggest her sworn statement was inaccurate." The draft quotes "distributed in early 2025" in depth 'where-transcript-sits' but never says to whom, and never connects it to the two-year gap.
flags.resolution: where-transcript-sits layer adds the FAQ line that the parties 'have an opportunity to review the full investigative record'; step 8 body keeps the DA's nearly-two-years point; a new open question asks whether the DA's office was told the Title IX files included the transcript and what contact the institutions had with her side before the lawsuit.

flags.note: The body pairs "'I can say with 100% confidence I was raped' and that she was 'physically hit very, very hard'" and then adds: "The same transcript has her calling the initial encounter 'pretty OK'." In the cited CBS report, the hitting remark comes right after she says she was "pretty OK with all of this" about the initial encounter: "And then, of course, I was being hit at the same time. Physically hit very, very hard." The draft's order separates the hitting from the encounter she described as consensual. That context matters for the forcible-compulsion question at the center of the DA's analysis.
flags.resolution: Step 1 body now quotes the initial-encounter answer in CBS order: 'as much as I can be because, again, I was super drunk ... But I was pretty OK with all of this,' then 'being hit at the same time.'

flags.note: The body uses AP's 'True' rating ("closed the case without speaking with her or reading a transcript") but leaves out the context in the same AP item: "Van Houten has said he believed the woman's statement, as relayed by the police, was detailed enough that he didn't see a need for more investigation" and "the information he received from campus police appeared at the time to be a comprehensive account." It also leaves out the DA's description of the request: CUPD asked his office "to review a statement ... to determine if her allegations constituted a crime under New York law," which he calls "common practice" for "legally technical matters such as ... 'lack of consent.'" Within the step, ABC's rebuttal is again placed after the DA's "nothing to review" explanation.
flags.resolution: Step 3 body adds AP's note that the DA said the statement was detailed enough that he saw no need for more investigation; the da-no-parallel-investigation quote context adds his 'common practice' description of the review request.

flags.note: The Cornell FAQ, a primary source the draft already cites, says: "Chi Phi, Xi Chapter was closed in 2024 and remains barred from campus." The draft only says the chapter was placed "under a temporary suspension order" (starting fact report-and-chapter-suspension and step 6). "Remains barred" appears only in a single timeline entry. The closure is one of my side's core facts. Also, the Nov. 8 suspension is confirmed by Cornell's own Nov. 26, 2024 letter, so the starting fact could be rated 'established' rather than 'reported'.
flags.resolution: Step 6 body opens with the FAQ's 'was closed in 2024 and remains barred from campus.' The starting fact stays 'reported' because her Nov. 8 police visit rests on AP.

flags.note: The body ends: "ABC News reports the Title IX results were not shared with Tompkins County prosecutors, 'who had declined to bring charges months earlier.'" This rebuttal closes my side's strongest Cornell step and reads as if not sharing was a choice. The FERPA limit is in step 7 depth but not here: disclosure without consent requires a judicial order or lawfully issued subpoena. The step also notes the 'late last week' versus Nov. 8 timing discrepancy in Cornell's own account, which adds doubt inside a step that favors Cornell.
flags.resolution: ABC's not-shared line moved to the middle of step 6's body, so the step ends on the AP rating and the court ruling. The FERPA limits stay in step 7's privacy layer and step 9's body.

flags.note: My side's step on the lawsuit-versus-statement difference repeats the other side's best line a third time. It appeared in step 1's body and the fell-short steelman, and here: "the 2024 transcript records her saying she was 'completely and totally incapacitated' and 'I can say with 100% confidence I was raped'." The step then ends with "Police told her of the DA's decision on Jan. 21, 2025, records show; her attorney says she believed until then that police were still investigating." That repeats step 3 and serves only to blunt the DA's 'nearly two years' point. The step is rated impact 'medium' even though the DA gives this difference as the reason he reopened the case.
flags.resolution: Step 8 no longer repeats the '100% confidence' and 'completely and totally incapacitated' lines (they are in step 1). The attorney's account of what she was told stays as the direct reply to the DA's no-contact point. Impact left at medium; owner may raise it (open issue).

flags.note: Starting fact 'state-takes-case' shortens EO 64 to "concerns about 'conflict or bias'." The order's text says: "concerns have been raised, both by Jane Doe and the public, that this incident cannot be fully and thoroughly investigated or prosecuted without conflict or bias, or the public perception of conflict or bias." It makes no finding of an actual conflict and names none. It also says the DA "relied, at least in part" on the statement, and it qualifies the omission with "reportedly." As shortened, the first thing readers see suggests the governor found bias.
flags.resolution: Starting fact state-takes-case now quotes 'conflict or bias, or the public perception' and says the concerns were raised by her and the public; step 11 says the order names no specific conflict and uses 'relying at least in part'.

flags.note: The confidence labels are uneven. 'Disputed' is on three of the five acted-reasonably steps (da-legal-reading, lawsuit-account-differs, consent-law-gap) and on none of the fell-short steps. consent-law-gap's headline rests on statute text (penal-law-130-00, primary) and the governor's own words (gov-transcript, official), which can be established. By contrast, da-reviewed-statement-only rests on contested accounts but is rated only 'reported.' Those accounts include "was rebuffed" against the DA's "nothing to review," and Cornell's earlier statements that it shared "all investigatory information" and "the results of the school's investigation."
flags.resolution: Step 3 relabelled 'disputed' (its Nov. 25 account is contested), the same standard as steps 4, 8 and 10. consent-law-gap stays 'disputed' because its body sets out the contested question of whether her drug use was voluntary.

flags.note: Open questions: seven of the eight probe possible institutional failures, for example "Who at Cornell police decided...", "why was she told of it on Jan. 21, 2025", "Did Cornell police collect..." and "How does Cornell Health account...". None asks the questions my side would raise. Examples: why neither she nor her attorneys brought the transcript or any correction to the DA in nearly two years, as the DA's statement records; whether the attorney general, applying the same Penal Law 130.00 rule, can reach a different legal result; and whether the governor's proposed legislative change could affect a 2024 case at all.
flags.resolution: Open question 3 now asks whether the attorney general can reach a different result under the same law; a new open question asks about contact between the institutions and her side before the lawsuit, whether the DA knew the Title IX files held the transcript, and whether a law change could reach a 2024 case.

flags.note: The headline "The DA's office declined charges within days" stresses haste. The decision came on Nov. 25, 2024, ten days after she signed the statement. ABC describes the date as "more than a month after" the alleged attack. Suggested neutral wording: "On Nov. 25, 2024, ten days after she signed the statement, the DA's office declined charges..."
flags.resolution: Step 3 headline now reads 'By Nov. 25, 2024, the DA's office had declined charges ...'.

flags.note: The depth section 'attorney-on-interview' sets out the attorney's claim that she was not contacted by investigators "trained in interviewing rape survivors" and a former prosecutor's criticism. It ends: "The sources cited here do not say whether anyone present had such training." But the body says a victim advocate was in the room, the NYT says she had "a support person ... and an adviser to explain her rights," and the Cornell FAQ describes its Title IX investigators as "a trained investigator." The signed attestation is the basis of the DA's review, yet this step is rated impact 'medium' while step 1 is 'high'.
flags.resolution: attorney-on-interview layer now notes a Title IX investigator and a victim advocate were present on the first day before saying the sources do not show anyone's training. Impact unchanged.

flags.note: The body ends with the mayor's "failed to contact or coordinate any response." The countervailing points are only in the depth section: Cornell referred the case to the DA, the county prosecutor whose county "includes Ithaca," and no cited source names a rule requiring Ithaca police to be notified. Move the depth line "The sources cited here do not ... identify a rule requiring it" into the body, or end on a neutral line.
flags.resolution: Step 5 body now says the sources cited identify no rule requiring Cornell police to notify city police.

flags.note: "CNN reports university officials confirmed two students named in the suit are still enrolled; the sources cited here do not say which sanctions those two received" invites an inference the sources do not support. The step's own material shows the two lightest-sanctioned men were accused of entering the room later, and one was found not responsible for sexual assault (CNY Central). The step is labeled 'neutral' even though its main content is AP rating the essay-only claim 'Misleading' and the two expulsions.
flags.resolution: Kept: the clause states a limit of the sources; without it the enrollment line invites the opposite inference. The sanction details for the two lightest-sanctioned men are in the lesser-finding layer. Step stays neutral because the red teams disagree on its direction.

flags.note: Depth 'before-report' puts claims about events before her report into the step about the interview and statement: the chapter's alleged ketamine history, the 2022 alerts, and the Cornell Health visit with "DNA evidence was gone." The dive's question is about how the report was handled. Cornell's reply is shown only as "At this time, we have no new information," which reads as a non-answer. Consider moving this to a separate, clearly labeled section on what happened before the report.
flags.resolution: Kept in depth and labelled 'alleged and reported'; Cornell's reply is quoted as given. Moving it to its own step would change the balance; left to the owner.

flags.note: The DA's reopening is presented only through the quote "Seeking justice sometimes requires us to reconsider or reopen cases." His Sept. 28 statement also says he had "already begun that process, starting with our conversation with Jane Doe and her attorneys," and assigned "a senior prosecutor ... who has significant experience in prosecuting sex crimes" to prepare a grand jury presentation. That shows the reopening was under way before he was replaced.
flags.resolution: da-reopening quote context now says he had 'already begun that process, starting with our conversation with Jane Doe and her attorneys' and asked a senior prosecutor to prepare a grand jury presentation.

bias_reports.summary: Red-team read of draft-r2 from the "institutions fell short" side. The overall structure is fair. There are 5 fell-short steps and 5 acted-reasonably steps, matched on impact. Fell-short opens the dive (step 1) and holds the penultimate step (governor-replaces-da). No judging adjectives or names of private individuals appear in user-facing copy. The problems are in which quotes the draft picks. The draft's own evidence quotes contain lines from the transcript and the Times that help this side, and the user-facing copy drops them: - "pretty OK" appears twice without the same sentence's "as much as I can be because, again, I was super drunk when I got there." - "completely and totally incapacitated" is kept out of the step about the omission. - The investigator's "eh, I'm tired" question is softened. - The Times's main finding, that the statement "left out key context" about her state of mind, is replaced by the Times's two mitigating lines. The DA's own later admissions appear only in depth boxes, while his defenses appear in step bodies: - "we were not provided the full picture by the University" - "we absolutely should have been informed" Several steps also give the other side the last word or the headline framing: - The sanctions step ends on AP's "Misleading" rating of a claim the lawsuit does not make. - The signed-statement headline uses her "I'm very confident about this." - A starting fact marked established gives Cornell's own summary of its sanctions. - The acted-reasonably steelman presents the DA's paraphrase ("the sexual conduct stopped") as if it were the statement's own words. I checked the flagged items against the existing source snapshots for CBS NY, the DA's Sept. 28 statement, the NYT takeaways and sanctions pieces, the AP fact check, explainer and 'misled' pieces, the NBC records piece, ABC, and the governor's transcript.

flags.note: Body: "The same transcript has her calling the initial encounter 'pretty OK'". The cited CBS transcript sentence is "Yeah, as much as I can be because, again, I was super drunk when I got there ... But I was pretty OK with all of this." The draft cuts the intoxication qualifier, though this exact quote is in the step's own evidence. The body adds the exculpatory 'I think it's "I'm tired"' but leaves out the next sentence in the same CBS report, "She also said she was 'completely and totally incapacitated'" (also in the AP fact check). That line only reaches user-facing copy in step 8 and in the steelman. In the core omission step, a reader sees every mitigating transcript line and loses the capacity line that most directly cuts against the DA's 'voluntary, conscious' reading.
flags.resolution: Step 1 body now gives 'pretty OK' with its qualifier ('as much as I can be because, again, I was super drunk when I got there') and adds 'completely and totally incapacitated' and 'It was coercion.'

flags.note: The step cites the Times only for lines that soften the omission: the statement 'made clear' she felt some of it was a crime, and the omissions 'may help explain' the DA's view. It drops the same article's headline finding, "Jane Doe's statement sent to the district attorney left out key context," and its description: "the official statement omits much of the context about Jane Doe's state of mind, her history as a sexual assault survivor and her thoughts as she was processing what was happening to her." The draft narrows the omission to "neither 'raped' line." AP's explainer, which the draft cites elsewhere, also reports the DA "contended Cornell's police had withheld key information." Leaving these out makes the condensation look like a two-line gap rather than the broad loss of context that independent reporting describes.
flags.resolution: Step 1 body adds the Times's finding that the statement 'omits much of the context about Jane Doe's state of mind'; the DA's 'we were not provided the full picture by the University' is now in step 11's body.

flags.note: The body softens the investigator's question to "asked whether she told one man 'no' or that she was tired." The CBS transcript reads: "Was it 'no' or was it, 'eh, I'm tired'?" The investigator's dismissive 'eh' bears directly on how her account was condensed by the same person who wrote the statement. The same CBS passage says she "swatted one man's hand away and told him she was uncomfortable, and she told another man no a few times or that she was too tired"; that is pushed to depth while her hedged answer stays in the body. Meanwhile the investigator's reassuring line, that his questions might sound accusatory but he needed specific answers 'to determine the right charges', is placed in the pro-police step statement-reviewed-and-signed.
flags.resolution: The investigator's question is quoted verbatim in the more-from-interview layer ('Was it "no" or was it, "eh, I'm tired"?'); the softened paraphrase was removed from the body.

flags.note: The fell-short lead step's body ends with Cornell's rebuttal: "a Cornell spokesperson ... said Cornell 'shared all investigatory information' with the DA's office." The step doesn't say that Cornell later removed this line from its FAQ (shown only in step 9). The first depth item is the DA's dismissive "that is a legal conclusion," and his admissions to CBS in the same interview are unused: "that changes the landscape for me" and "Nobody knows this information about the transcript." On the dive's strongest fell-short point, the institutions' framing gets the last word.
flags.resolution: Step 1 body now notes the 'all investigatory information' wording was since removed from the FAQ; the da-legal-conclusion context adds 'changes the landscape for me.'

flags.note: Headline: "She reviewed, annotated and signed the six-page statement ... saying, 'I'm very confident about this'." The pull-quote doesn't appear in the body. Placed right after the omission step, it shifts responsibility for what the statement left out onto her. The step doesn't say that no cited source shows she was told this condensed document would be the only thing prosecutors read; the draft itself lists that as an open question. The CBS detail that the adviser offered to review the statement, with no recorded answer, is in depth only. Her earlier '100% confidence I was raped' from the same interview isn't mentioned alongside it.
flags.resolution: Step 2 headline no longer leads with 'I'm very confident about this'; the body adds that the sources do not say whether she was told the statement would be the main document prosecutors reviewed.

flags.note: In the step built to show her account changed, the body again uses the truncated quote: "in 2024 she said she was 'pretty OK' with the first encounter ... while the suit says she was 'incapable of consenting'." The draft drops "as much as I can be because, again, I was super drunk when I got there" (CBS) and the Times's own wording, "Things had started off consensual — though she was drunk." With the qualifier, the 2024 and 2026 accounts are much closer than the step suggests. The DA's charge that "neither she nor her attorneys contacted his office in nearly two years" is answered only by "her attorney says she believed until then that police were still investigating." The draft leaves out the AP-reported claim that, when she was told of the decision, she was told "they weren't going to prosecute, but they were still investigating," and that her lawyer "thought they were still investigating". That explains the silence after Jan. 2025, which the DA's line leaves unexplained.
flags.resolution: Step 8 body now uses the Times's 'had started off consensual — though she was drunk' and gives the attorney's account that she was told 'they weren't going to prosecute, but they were still investigating' right after the DA's no-contact point.

flags.note: This acted-reasonably step is about whether the private complainant's accounts are consistent. That goes to her credibility, not to how the institutions handled the 2024 report: the Nov. 2024 decision could not have depended on a 2026 lawsuit. Under this case's rule that the dive's question must be about the institutional response, the headline "The DA and the Times say the 2026 lawsuit describes her ability to consent differently" turns her consistency into a defense of the institutions. The Times's counterweight, that the suit "recount[s] the same events," is in the body but not the headline.
flags.resolution: Kept: the DA gives the difference between the lawsuit and the statement as his reason for reopening, so the step bears on the institutions' 2026 decisions, and it is marked disputed. Headline now carries the Times's point that both accounts 'recount the same events.' Owner decision noted as an open issue.

flags.note: The DA's strongest admissions against Cornell appear only in depth boxes. "It has become clear that we were not provided the full picture by the University" is a depth quote here, and "we absolutely should have been informed" is a depth quote in faq-revised. Neither is in any step body or in the fell-short steelman. His defenses are in bodies: steps 3, 4 and 8, plus the starting fact no-charges-2024. Cornell's president's "must do better" is likewise only in depth contexts and the timeline. A reader skimming bodies sees the DA defend himself repeatedly but never sees him blame the university.
flags.resolution: The DA's 'we were not provided the full picture by the University' is now in step 11's body and the fell-short steelman; 'we absolutely should have been informed' stays as a step 9 quote layer.

flags.note: The headline ends "Cornell disputes the essay claim," yet the NYT summaries in the body show four of the seven had to write reflection papers. Two of those four got only training plus papers. The body then closes on "An AP fact check rated as 'Misleading' the claim that essays were Cornell's only punishment." That was a social-media claim. The lawsuit alleges the students were "afforded the opportunity to mitigate their conduct by submitting essays," not that essays were the only punishment. The step is labeled 'neutral' but is built as a rebuttal, and the last word goes to a debunking of a claim this side doesn't make. Her attorney's point that all but two can still graduate is only in depth.
flags.resolution: Step 7 body now says AP rated a claim made online, not the lawsuit's allegation, and no longer ends on that rating.

flags.note: The body repeats the DA's selected line, that she thought she 'had already done Ketamine once so why not do it a second time' before she 'snorted the line', to show voluntariness. It omits the statement's own explanation, reported by the Times, CNN and ABC: "I had become extremely uncomfortable with how this night was turning out, so my thought was, if I do ketamine again, maybe I will pass out ... then they could be charged with rape." The Times says the summary "explains that one reason she took the drug ketamine was to escape it." That context appears only in the step-4 depth box. In the step on whether her drug use was voluntary, the body reproduces the DA's selective quote.
flags.resolution: Step 10 body adds the Times's report that the statement says she took more ketamine hoping to pass out so the men 'could be charged with rape.'

flags.note: The steelman says "the statement says that each time she asked to stop, 'the sexual conduct stopped.'" Those quoted words are the DA's characterization ("According to the statement, each time Jane Doe asked to stop the sexual conduct, the sexual conduct stopped"), not text from her statement. The DA's own excerpt of the statement contradicts the gloss: a man "reached for the area near [her] vagina several times and each time he did, [she] would swat his hand away," and later "again tried reaching." A steelman may argue a case, but it shouldn't attribute the DA's paraphrase to her.
flags.resolution: Acted-reasonably steelman now reads 'the DA says that, according to the statement, each time she asked to stop, "the sexual conduct stopped."'

flags.note: Before any step, an 'established' starting fact gives Cornell's own summary: "a hearing panel of trained faculty and staff heard evidence over multiple days and issued sanctions that included expulsions and suspensions." It leaves out that, per the discipline summaries, two men got only training and reflection papers, that two named students remain enrolled, and that the sanctions are disputed in the lawsuit. Similarly, starting fact report-and-chapter-suspension adopts Cornell's claim that student suspensions were issued "when the conduct was reported." Cornell's own Nov. 26, 2024 letter says they were issued "late last week," a conflict noted only later, in step 6.
flags.resolution: Starting fact separate-title-ix-process adds that the lawsuit disputes how some students were sanctioned; report-and-chapter-suspension adds the Nov. 26 letter's 'late last week.'

flags.note: The headline enlists the governor for the acted-reasonably view: "the governor calls this 'a gap in State law'." It drops her framing that the case "also exposed another problem." In the same remarks she said "at every turn, she was failed by people and institutions" and "No institution gets to protect its reputation at the expense of a young person seeking justice." The body includes 'also exposed another problem', but the headline reads as if the governor sees the law as the core issue.
flags.resolution: Step 10 headline now quotes the governor's 'also exposed another problem'; the body keeps 'a gap in State law.'

flags.note: The body describes the revised FAQ as saying police shared the statement and screenshot, "which matches what the DA says he received." That reads as validating Cornell's correction rather than flagging the retraction. The body then ends on Cornell's defenses: 'the FAQ is a living document' and the FERPA privacy line. The step is also rated only 'medium' impact, though it concerns Cornell's public account of what it gave prosecutors.
flags.resolution: Step 9 body reordered to close on the conflicting accounts of what reached prosecutors; 'which matches' changed to 'the same items the DA says he received.' Impact unchanged.

flags.note: The final step's body closes on an accused student's motion to void the attorney general's appointment, "citing a social media post supporting the former student." The AG's response, that the investigation will be "guided only by the facts, the evidence, and the law," is only in depth. The dive's last substantive note is a challenge to the special prosecutor's impartiality.
flags.resolution: Step 12 body now opens with the motion to void and the attorney general's 'guided only by the facts' reply and ends on the pending reviews.

flags.note: The Cornell Health allegation sits only in a depth box ('Before her police report'). NBC's records piece adds the attorney's specific claim, missing from the draft, that had the health center referred her for an exam there "might have been recoverable DNA because she was there within 48 hours," and his description of this as "the first failure post assault." It's labeled as allegation, but it's the only pre-report institutional contact, and it's out of the main flow.
flags.resolution: before-report layer adds the attorney's NBC claim about recoverable DNA and 'the first failure post assault', labelled as his allegation.

fact_check.claim: On Sept. 16, 2026 a former student sued in N.Y. Supreme Court, New York County, alleging sexual assault by multiple people at the Chi Phi house on Oct. 19-20, 2024; defendants include Cornell, Chi Phi entities and seven members.
fact_check.note: EO 64 and the complaint (clerk stamp 09/16/2026, Index 161704/2026) support the filing date, court and dates. The caption lists Cornell, three Chi Phi entities and seven individual members among other defendants, so "include" is accurate. Court record plus official order: established is correct.
fact_check.quote: WHEREAS, on September 16, 2026, Jane Doe filed a lawsuit in the Supreme Court, New York County, alleging she was the victim of a sexual assault perpetrated by multiple individuals occurring on October 19-20, 2024;

fact_check.claim: AP reports she first went to Cornell police on Nov. 8, 2024, about three weeks after the night in question; that day the chapter was suspended and a crime alert went out; Cornell says student suspensions were issued when the conduct was reported.

Cornell's Nov. 26 letter confirms the Nov. 8 suspension order, the Cornell Sun confirms the Friday crime alert, and the FAQ supports the student suspensions as Cornell's claim. Mix of news and official sources: reported is correct. Editor (final): this text was revised after this check; the new wording was re-verified only by check_quotes.py and a quoted-fragment check.
